conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You were brought in today because of weakness and confusion. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been really weak since this morning. I felt confused when I woke up. I’ve been trying to stay hydrated like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your calcium level came back high at 10.7, which can cause confusion and weakness. This is related to your multiple myeloma. We’ll start IV fluids right away to help bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they gave me pamidronate. Why not this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had that treatment less than a week ago, so we can’t repeat it yet. Instead, we’ll use nasal calcitonin and fluids. It works quickly and safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My sugars have been high too—my wife said I was over 600 last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood sugar was 358 when you arrived. The steroids you received in clinic can make that worse. We’ll monitor closely and adjust your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on glargine at night. Should I keep that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep your glargine and add a sliding scale. Our diabetes team will help fine-tune it. You may need more insulin while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. My kidneys were a little off last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.3 today, which is slightly elevated. We’ll give fluids carefully and avoid any medications that could hurt your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your calcium is coming down. We’ll keep the IV fluids going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit more alert today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely because your calcium is improving. We also checked a chest X-ray—no pneumonia, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a bit of a cough. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from dryness or irritation. Your flu test was negative, and cultures didn’t show infection. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar spiked to over 450 yesterday. We put you on a short insulin drip to get it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize it got that high. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it stays high. But we caught it quickly. You’re back on subcutaneous insulin now, and we’ve increased your glargine to 35 units at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll check my sugars more often at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re giving you a new glucometer and strips. Please check four times a day—fasting and after meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine went up to 1.7, but it’s now back down to 1.2. That’s a good sign your kidneys are recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Dehydration and high calcium can stress the kidneys. We’ve been careful with your fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling short of breath when I walk to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. It could be from a bit of fluid buildup, but your chest X-ray showed only mild changes. We’ve held back fluids to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be another blood clot? I had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a fair concern. We did a V/Q scan, and it showed a low chance of a pulmonary embolism. Your heart rhythm and EKG were normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be related to your myeloma or anemia. But given your history, we want to rule out heart issues. We’ve ordered a stress test after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I should call to schedule that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please call the cardiology office this week. It’s a pharmacologic test, so you won’t need to walk on a treadmill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You mentioned more shortness of breath yesterday. We did a portable chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any new fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No new pleural fluid or pneumothorax. Your Port-A-Cath is in good position. We think your symptoms may be chronic from your overall condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do get tired easily these days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with advanced myeloma. We’re continuing your bortezomib and dexamethasone to control the disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your calcium is now 9.5—well within normal range. Great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. And my sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Much better—around 250. Still high, but stable. Keep checking at home and call your endocrinologist if it goes above 180 or below 80.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about the vancomycin I’m on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing it every six hours to prevent C. diff, especially since you’ve had it before and are on multiple medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been constipated though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can adjust your stool softeners. Let the nurse know if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re planning to discharge you today. Your calcium is normal, and you’re feeling more like yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your blood sugar four times daily. Take your new insulin dose—35 units of glargine at bedtime. Call endocrinology if sugars are out of range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stress test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, call to schedule that. Also follow up with oncology. We may consider denosumab for your calcium if it keeps rising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I’ll stay on top of everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll send all instructions and prescriptions home with you. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam looks good—alert, breathing well, no swelling. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is here for you. Call us if anything changes. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your discharge labs are back. Hemoglobin is 7.3, which is low but stable. We’re not transfusing unless you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. I’ll watch for fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. And remember, if you feel dizzy or very short of breath, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will be here soon to take you home. Do you have any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Check sugars, call endocrinology, schedule stress test, follow up with oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re cleared for discharge. The vancomycin will now be four times a day at home, not every six hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Four times a day.
